excerpt: What each part does, how to switch it on, and how to move the pointer without fear. A calm first hour for anyone who has never used a computer.

body.text: This lesson teaches you the parts of a computer, how to switch it on, and how to type your first words. If you have never used one, that is a normal place to start. Nobody was born knowing this, and nothing in this lesson can damage the machine.

A computer has four parts you can see, and each one has a job. The tower, or the laptop body, stores your work and does the thinking. The monitor shows what is happening. The keyboard lets you type. The mouse lets you point. Most people who say they cannot use a computer were never shown these four parts by name.

body.alt: A desktop computer on a wooden desk with a monitor, keyboard and mouse.
body.caption: Four parts, four jobs. When something feels wrong later, check these first, before you decide the machine is finished.

body.text: Before you start

items: A desktop computer or a laptop with its charger.
A wall socket that is switched on.
About thirty minutes without hurry.
Permission to use the machine, if it is not yours.

body.text: Sit down and take your time. Rushing is what makes a first lesson feel like an examination, and the machine can wait for you.
Check the cables, then switch on
A computer that looks dead is usually only disconnected. This is the first thing to check, and it is also the first thing people skip, because they assume they broke something.

items: Follow each cable from the wall socket to the machine, and push it in gently.
Check that the wall socket is switched on at the wall.
Press the round power button once, then take your finger away.
Wait. Twenty seconds of nothing is normal.
Stop at the sign-in screen or the desktop.

body.text: You will see the maker's logo, sometimes a spinning circle, then a sign-in screen or a desktop with a picture and small icons. The screen may stay dark for part of that time. If it is still black after a minute, look at the monitor's own power light, then the socket, before you press anything again.
It looks like nothing is happening while it starts. The machine is working, and pressing the power button again only makes it begin the same job twice.
If a password box appears and the computer is not yours, ask the owner before you type. Guessing can lock the account, and nobody needs that worry on their first day.
Move the pointer without fear
Rest your hand on the mouse and slide it slowly. Watch the small arrow on the screen. That arrow is the pointer, and it is your hand, drawn.
Keep your wrist on the desk. When you reach the edge of the desk, lift the mouse, put it back in the middle, and keep sliding. The pointer stays where it is while the mouse is in the air.
One press of the left button is a click. Two quick presses are a double-click, which opens things. A right-click opens a short menu, and it is not an error. Click an empty space to close it.
Most beginners press too hard and click too slowly. The mouse needs no force, and the two clicks need to be close together. If a folder does not open, try again faster rather than harder.

body.alt: A right hand resting on a computer mouse beside a keyboard.
body.caption: Rest the heel of your hand on the desk and slide. One press is a click. Two quick presses open a file.

body.text: Type your first words
You will type in Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on a Mac. Both open a plain white page with nothing to distract you, which is what a first lesson needs.

items: On Windows, press the Windows key, type Notepad, then press Enter.
On a Mac, press Command and Space, type TextEdit, then press Enter.
Click once inside the white page so that a blinking line appears.
Type your full name slowly, using the long bar for a space.
Press Enter for a new line, and Backspace to remove the letter before the cursor.
Close the window with the X. If it asks about saving, choose Don't Save. Saving is the next lesson.

body.text: A blinking line appears where you click. That line is the cursor, and your next letter lands there. If you do not see it, click once inside the white area again.
Do not worry about speed. Hunting for each letter is how everybody starts, and accuracy is the habit worth building first.
If it goes wrong
Every one of these has a cause you can check, and none of them means you have broken the computer.

items: The screen stays black: check the monitor's power light, the wall socket, then the cable at the back.
The pointer does not move: check the mouse cable, or turn the mouse over and look for a light. A wireless mouse may need new batteries.
Every letter comes out in capitals: Caps Lock is on. Press it once and look for the small light on the key.
The screen is too dark: find the brightness key with a sun symbol, usually on the top row.
The machine ignores everything: hold the power button for ten seconds to switch it off. Wait, then press it once to start again.
A message asks for a password you do not have: stop and call the owner. Do not install anything a message tells you to install.

body.text: Practice
Ten minutes today is enough to start. Ten minutes tomorrow is what makes it stay.

items: Name the four parts out loud, without looking back at this page.
Move the pointer to each corner of the screen and back to the middle.
Open Notepad and type your name, your town, and today's date.
Close the program without saving, then open it and type the same line again.
Switch off properly: Start menu, power symbol, Shut down.

body.text: You can now start a computer, move the pointer, click, and type. That is a real skill, and every later lesson stands on it. In the next lesson you will learn where your work is kept, so that nothing you type has to disappear again.
